Hook: In March 1981, a drilling crew was working in the Atacama desert of northern Chile, the driest place on Earth, for an exploration project of two American companies, Utah International and Getty Oil. They were looking for copper hidden in the bedrock beneath the gravel. They had money for nine holes. The first came up empty. So did the second, the third, the fourth and the fifth. More than half the money was gone, and there was nothing to show for it. They moved the rig to a low hill and drilled the sixth hole. It was finished on the fourteenth of March, and it went through rock rich in copper. The first careful estimate was 300 million tonnes of ore at well over one percent copper. The whole search, two years of it, had cost 3 million dollars. They called it Escondida: Spanish for hidden.

The hill became Escondida. It opened in 1991, built to produce three hundred and twenty thousand tonnes of copper a year, and it grew into the largest copper mine on Earth. In the year to June 2025 it produced 1,305 thousand tonnes, and earned 8.6 billion dollars of operating profit for its owners: BHP, Rio Tinto and a group of Japanese partners. But the rock is getting poorer. The ore going into its mills held 1.02 percent copper last year. This year, about 0.85. So BHP expects output to fall, to under a million tonnes a year by the end of the decade, while the cost of each pound rises. A mine is a bet of billions on a price decades away, made on rock that only gets worse.
Industry, Built. Part nine: mining and metals. Why is a mine worth a fortune in one decade and nothing in the next?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: build, wait, or sell.

Play it yourself. You own one copper deposit, found by your own geologists. It holds 600 million tonnes of ore, and each tonne holds half a percent of copper: five kilograms in a tonne of rock. A mill could process forty million tonnes a year for fifteen years, making about 174 thousand tonnes of copper in the first year, and less after that, because the best rock is mined first. It would cost three billion dollars and three years to build. Producing a pound of copper would cost about 1 dollar 97 at first, rising to 2 dollars 43. Add the building cost, the royalty and the tax, and the mine pays its way, at an eight percent return, if copper sells for 3 dollars 61 a pound over its whole life. Copper sells for 4 dollars 50 today. You have three choices. Build now. Wait a year and see where the price goes, then build only if it still pays. Or sell the deposit to a bigger miner, which offers 784 million dollars in cash today. Pause, and choose.

Before you choose, look at what a mine is, in cash. For three years it is only a cost: a billion dollars a year, and no copper. Then it pays, year after year, but a little less each year, because the grade falls and the mill makes less copper from the same rock. At the end, someone has to close it, fill the holes and treat the water, and that costs money too. At 4 dollars 50 a pound, the running total turns positive only in year 7. Everything is paid up front, and the reward comes over a decade and a half, at prices nobody knows yet. That is the shape of every mine on Earth.

Now let the price move, as it does. Here are forty of four hundred futures, each starting at four fifty and wandering, with shocks every year, back towards three eighty, roughly where copper has spent the last few years. Run the mine through all four hundred. If you build now, the mine is worth 859 million dollars on average, in today's money. But each dot is one future, and in 32 percent of them, the red ones, the mine loses money. If you wait a year, you avoid some of the bad futures, but you give up a year of high prices, and here that costs more than it saves: 652 million on average. If you sell, you get 784 million, whatever happens. So the answer depends on who you are. A giant with twenty mines can take the average, because its bad futures and good futures cancel out across the mines. A small company with one deposit and a bank loan cannot survive the one future in three that goes wrong, so it should sell. That is how the industry is built: small explorers find deposits, and the majors buy them and build them.
Process: Chapter two. From rock to metal.

Copper does not come out of the ground as metal. It comes as a mineral, mostly copper and iron and sulphur, spread through rock as grains you can barely see. So the mine blasts the rock and digs it, and trucks the size of houses haul it out of the pit. Crushers break it into gravel. Huge rotating mills, full of steel balls, grind it finer than sand, because every grain of copper mineral must be set free from the rock around it. Then comes the trick that makes modern mining possible: flotation. The powder is mixed with water and chemicals that make the copper minerals repel water, air is blown through, and the copper grains cling to the bubbles and rise to the top as a froth, while the waste sinks. The froth, dried, is concentrate: from about one percent copper to about a quarter or a third. Concentrate is light enough to ship, and much of it crosses an ocean, to smelters in China, Japan and elsewhere. A smelter melts it and burns off the sulphur and iron, leaving plates that are about ninety-nine percent copper. A refinery hangs those plates in an acid bath and runs an electric current through it, and pure copper builds up on the other side: cathode, ninety-nine point nine nine percent copper, the metal the world trades.

Now count the tonnes. Take ore at one percent copper, about what Escondida milled last year. To make one tonne of copper, the mill has to process about 118 tonnes of ore, because the ore is one percent copper and the mill recovers only about eighty-five percent of that. But an open pit cannot take only the ore. To reach it, the mine strips away the waste rock around and above it, here two tonnes of waste for every tonne of ore. So the mine moves about 353 tonnes of rock for each tonne of copper. The mill turns that into about 3.6 tonnes of concentrate, and the smelter and refinery turn that into one tonne of metal. Each square here has an area in proportion to its tonnes. Almost everything a copper mine does is moving and grinding rock that is not copper. That is why the costs of a mine are mostly diesel, electricity, water, tyres, steel balls and wages, and why they depend so much on how much copper is in each tonne.

There is a second route, for poorer ore and for ores where the copper has already been changed by air and water. The rock is crushed and stacked in great heaps on a waterproof liner, and weak acid is sprinkled over it for months. The acid dissolves the copper and trickles out at the bottom as a blue-green solution. A chemical step concentrates it, and an electric current plates the copper straight out as cathode, at the mine. No mill, no flotation, no smelter, so it is cheap per tonne of rock, and it can make money from rock that a mill never could. Freeport's mines in Arizona and New Mexico put ore holding just 0.21 percent copper on their leach pads in 2025. At that grade, a tonne of copper needs more than 560 tonnes of ore. A copper mine, in other words, is a machine for moving rock cheaply, and what decides whether it pays is how much copper each tonne holds.
Grade: Every square here is a tonne of rock, four hundred tonnes in all. Grade is the share of each tonne that is copper. At three percent, a very rich ore, twelve of the four hundred tonnes would be copper. At one percent, roughly what Escondida milled last year, four. At half a percent, the grade of our model deposit, two. And at zero point two one percent, the grade of the ore that Freeport stacks on its leach pads in Arizona and New Mexico, less than one. Not one copper square in four hundred. The rock is mostly rock, and the miner pays to dig, haul and grind every tonne of it.

Turn that around, and ask how much rock it takes to make one tonne of copper. At three percent, about 39 tonnes of ore, or 118 tonnes of rock once you count the waste you strip to reach it. At one percent, three times as much. At half a percent, six times. At zero point two one percent, 1,681 tonnes of rock for a single tonne of copper. The rule is simple and brutal: halve the grade and you double the rock, and with it the diesel, the power, the water and the wear for every pound you sell.

Now put that into money. Take our model mine and change only the grade. The purple line is the cash cost of a pound of copper, and the gold line is the price the mine needs over its life to be worth building at all, once the three billion dollars of construction is paid back. At two percent, copper costs under a dollar a pound to produce, and the mine pays its way at about a dollar thirty. Slide down to one percent, and both rise slowly. Below half a percent they climb steeply, because the copper is shared out over ever more rock. The white line is what copper actually sold for on average in 2025. A deposit at a quarter of a percent is not worth building at that price, and a deposit at one percent is a fortune. The same hole, the same machines, the same people: grade decides which one you have.

This is happening right now at Escondida. In the year to June 2025, the ore going into its concentrators held 1.02 percent copper. This year BHP expects about 0.85. The mills grind roughly the same tonnage, so if nothing else changed, the copper would fall with the grade, by about a sixth. BHP's own guidance says the same: between 1,150 and 1,250 thousand tonnes this year, and nine hundred thousand to a million a year after that. And because the mine still moves and grinds all that rock, the cost of each pound rises, from 1 dollar 19 last year to between a dollar fifty and a dollar eighty. This is the treadmill every miner runs on. The best rock goes first, the grade falls every year, and the company must find new ore, or new ways to process old ore, just to stand still.
Plan: Chapter four. The mine plan, and the option to wait.

A mine is dug to a plan. Engineers drill the deposit on a grid, build a three-dimensional model of the grade, block by block, and then decide the order in which to dig it. An open pit grows in stages called pushbacks: each one widens and deepens the hole. Because money now is worth more than money later, the plan takes the richest, cheapest rock first. So in our model mine, output is highest in the first year, 174 thousand tonnes, and falls every year after, to 131. And the cost of a pound climbs, from 1 dollar 97 to 2 dollars 43. A mine's best years are its first. Every mine is a declining asset, and the plan makes it decline on purpose.

Now the hardest decision: when to build at all. Take the model deposit again, and ask what it is worth at different copper prices. The orange line is the value of building it now. It crosses zero at the break-even price, 3 dollars 61 a pound. Above that, building adds value; below it, building destroys it. The blue line is the value of something else: owning the deposit and keeping the right to build it next year, once you have seen the price. At break-even, building now is worth nothing, but the right to wait is worth about 616 million dollars. If the price rises, you build and keep the gain; if it falls, you leave the copper in the ground and lose nothing. The moment you build, that choice is gone, and so is its value. So the rule is not to build at break-even. Build when the price is well above it: here, at about 4 dollars 88, 35 percent higher, where building now finally beats waiting. Economists Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck made this idea the heart of a famous book on investment. It explains a pattern you will see again in this film. Miners approve new mines only in booms, when the price is far above their costs, and the mines arrive years later, often into a market that has turned.
Curve: Every mine has its own cost, and if you line them up from cheapest to dearest you get the industry's cost curve, the idea from Part four. The full curve, covering every mine on Earth, is sold by consultancies. Here are four real operations, drawn from what their owners publish. The width of each block is the copper it produced in 2025; the height is its net cash cost per pound. Escondida, as we saw, at about a dollar twenty. Freeport's mines in Peru and Chile, at about two forty, and its mines in Arizona and New Mexico, low grade and largely leached, at about three dollars. And Grasberg, in the mountains of Indonesian Papua, sits below zero. Its net cost is minus fifty-five cents a pound, because Grasberg is also one of the world's great gold mines, and Freeport subtracts the gold and silver it sells, at an average of three thousand four hundred dollars an ounce last year, from the cost of its copper. That is a by-product credit, and it can be worth more than the main product's costs. Copper averaged 4 dollars 51 a pound on the London Metal Exchange in 2025. Every mine here made money, and the green shows how much per pound. In September 2026 the price reached 6 dollars 56, and the margins doubled. But drop the price to two fifty, and the American mines lose money on every pound, while Grasberg barely notices. The low-cost mine is the one that survives the bad years, and that, not size, is a miner's moat.

And the curve does not stand still. Each mine's block changes shape as its grade falls. Here is Escondida last year: wide and low. This year, on BHP's guidance, a little narrower and taller. And on its outlook for the five years from 2027, narrower and taller again. A whole industry of mines is doing this at once, so the curve creeps upward, year after year. Unless new, richer deposits are found and built to replace them, the cost of the marginal pound of copper rises, and with it, over the long run, the price.
Where: Chapter six. Where metal comes from.

Copper is mined where geology put it, and refined where industry put the smelters, and those are not the same places. Here is the world's copper mining in 2025, from the US Geological Survey. Chile dug 5.3 million tonnes, the most of any country. Then Congo, whose copper belt runs into Zambia, then Peru, then China, Russia and the United States. In all, about 23 million tonnes. Now the refining. China refined 14 million tonnes of copper, from mines that dug only 1.8. China mines about 8 percent of the world's copper and refines about 48 percent of it. The rest of its supply arrives by sea, as concentrate and as part-refined copper from Chile, Peru, Congo and elsewhere, and as scrap. Notice too that the world refined about 6 million tonnes more copper than it mined. Copper does not wear out. Old wire, pipes and engines are melted down and refined again, and that is a large part of the supply. The country that refines the metal sets the terms on which the miners sell it, and that is a theme that will come back in the chapter on critical minerals.

How long can this last? The Geological Survey counts about 980 million tonnes of copper in the world's known reserves: about 43 years at today's rate of mining. That sounds like a countdown, but it is not one. As with oil in Part eight, a reserve is an economic number: copper that is known and worth mining at today's prices with today's methods. When the price rises or the methods improve, poorer rock becomes ore, and the reserves grow. People have been predicting that copper will run out within a few decades for a long time. What happens instead is that the grade falls, and the cost of the next tonne rises.
Iron: Chapter seven. Iron ore: three companies, one customer.

Copper is the metal of wires. Iron is the metal of everything else: steel for buildings, bridges, ships and cars. And iron ore is mined on a scale nothing else matches. The world produced about 2.6 billion tonnes of usable iron ore in 2025. Australia alone produced 980 million tonnes, most of it from the Pilbara in the north-west; Brazil 420, then India and China. Most of Australia's and Brazil's ore goes by sea to the steel mills of Asia, and above all to China, which makes more steel than the rest of the world combined. Three companies, Rio Tinto and BHP in Australia and Vale in Brazil, are the biggest sellers. You can see who the customer is from where the price is quoted. The standard price of iron ore is the price of a tonne of fines, sixty-two percent iron, delivered to a port in northern China: about 99 dollars a tonne in 2025.

That daily, delivered-to-China price is new. For about forty years, until the late 2000s, iron ore had one price a year. The big miners and the big steelmakers negotiated a benchmark each year, and everyone else followed it. Look at 2003: the same price in every month, 13 dollars 82 a tonne. Then China's steel industry grew so fast that much of its ore was bought on the spot market, at prices far above the benchmark, and the miners wanted those prices too. On the first of April 2010, Vale announced that almost all its customers, ninety-seven percent of them, had agreed to prices tied to the spot market and changed every quarter. The annual benchmark was finished. Now look at 2024: a different price every month, from 96 to 137 dollars. The risk that used to be negotiated away once a year is now carried by both sides, every day.

Here is the whole story in one line. Through the 1990s, iron ore cost about twelve to fifteen dollars a tonne, and the benchmark barely moved. Then China's boom. From fourteen dollars in 2003 the price rose more than tenfold in eight years. After 2010 it moved every month, falling to the fifties in 2015 and 2016, then soaring to a peak of 216 dollars in June 2021. It is now about 100. For the miners of the Pilbara, whose ore is among the cheapest in the world to dig and ship, even that is a very good price. Iron ore has been the richest business in mining for twenty years, and almost all of that wealth came from one customer.
Pricing: Chapter eight. How metals are priced.

Who decides what copper costs? Not the miner, and not the buyer. Follow the metal. The mine sells concentrate to a smelter, and the smelter and refinery sell cathode to the companies that make wire, tube and sheet. At both steps, the price comes from an exchange: the London Metal Exchange above all, and COMEX in New York and the Shanghai Futures Exchange, where traders buy and sell copper for delivery now and in the months ahead. The miner is paid the exchange price for the copper in its concentrate, minus charges for smelting and refining it. The buyer of cathode pays the exchange price plus a premium for delivery where it wants it. So every mine on Earth takes the same price, set every day by traders who will never see the ore. A miner cannot charge more because its copper is better: a tonne of cathode is a tonne of cathode. All it can choose is its cost.

And the price moves a great deal. Here is copper since 1992, in the dollars of each month. It sat near two thousand dollars a tonne for a decade, rose fourfold in the China boom of the 2000s, crashed in 2008, and has climbed in waves since. In September 2026 it averaged 14,473 dollars a tonne, about 6 dollars 56 a pound: the highest monthly average in this record. But a dollar of 1992 is not a dollar of today. Adjust for inflation, and the peak was Feb 2011, at about 15,028 of today's dollars. Copper is dear today, but not, after inflation, at its dearest. Always ask which dollars a record is counted in.

Normally the exchanges in London, New York and Shanghai quote almost the same price, because if they drift apart, traders buy in the cheap place and ship to the dear one. In 2025 that broke. The United States announced it would look into tariffs on imported copper, and nobody knew how high they would be, or when. COMEX copper, in New York, averaged 4 dollars 80 a pound, a record, against 4 dollars 51 on the London exchange. A gap of about thirty cents a pound is a fortune on a shipload, so traders raced to get copper into America before any tariff began. American imports of refined copper nearly doubled, from 903 thousand tonnes to about 1,700 thousand, far more than the country used. The price of a metal is set by traders, but it can still be bent by a single government.
Intermission: An intermission: one hundred and twenty years of copper, from the US Geological Survey's historical statistics, in constant dollars. The First World War sent it soaring, and the Depression sent it to the floor. It rose again with the electrification of the post-war world and peaked in the 1960s and early 70s. Then came thirty years of decline, to a low in 2002, as new mines in Chile and new methods like leaching flooded the market. And then China. Look at the ends: in constant dollars, a tonne cost about 3,980 in 2020, against 7,000 in 1900, after a century in which the world used more copper every decade. Demand rose enormously, and the industry kept finding ways to dig poorer rock more cheaply.

The story so far. A mine is billions of dollars spent up front and repaid over decades, at prices nobody knows. At one percent copper, the industry moves about three hundred and fifty tonnes of rock for every tonne of metal. The grade falls as the best rock is dug first, so output falls and costs rise. Waiting has value, so mines get built in booms. Every miner takes the exchange's price, and the low-cost mine is the one that survives. And Chile digs the most copper while China refines almost half of it. Next: the supercycle, the state's share, the critical minerals, gold, and the landscape.
Boom: Now the decade that made the modern mining industry. In 2002 copper and iron ore were cheap, and had been for twenty years. Miners had cut costs, closed mines and stopped exploring. Then China's economy, already growing fast, began to build at a scale the world had never seen: apartment blocks, railways, power grids, factories, whole new cities, all of them made of steel and wired with copper. Supply could not keep up, because, as we have seen, a new mine takes years to find, approve and build. So the price did the rationing. From 2002 to 2011, copper rose 5.7 times, and iron ore 13.2 times. Bankers called it a supercycle. And then the new mines approved in the boom arrived, just as China's building slowed. By 2016 copper had lost almost half its 2011 price, and iron ore two-thirds.

Watch what that did to the miners. Here are the three iron ore giants, year by year, from 2015. The bust came first. Iron ore fell to about fifty-six dollars a tonne in 2015, and all three reported losses, as they wrote down the value of mines, projects and other assets they had bought or built at the top. Vale lost 12.1 billion dollars. Then the price recovered, and profits came back. By 2021, with iron ore near 158 dollars, Vale earned 22.4 billion and Rio Tinto 21.1, and in its year to June 2022 BHP reported 30.9 billion, swollen by the profit from its oil business, which it merged into Woodside that year. See how much harder profits swing than the price. The miners' costs barely change when the price moves, so almost every extra dollar on the price is an extra dollar of margin, and every lost dollar comes out of it. A miner is a bet on the price, made with a fixed cost base: the cost curve of chapter five, multiplied by billions of tonnes.
State: Chapter ten. The state takes its share.

In almost every country outside the United States, the minerals under the ground belong to the state, not to whoever owns the land on top. A mining company is a tenant. It digs, and pays rent. Take everything our model mine sells over its life at four fifty a pound: about 23 billion dollars. Running the mine takes about half. Building it and closing it takes more. The state takes a royalty, a share of every dollar sold, and an income tax on the profit. What is left belongs to the owners. With a four percent royalty and a twenty-seven percent tax, the state takes about 36 percent of the mine's profit, and it takes the royalty even in years when the mine makes none. Many countries take far more: through bigger royalties, special mining taxes, or by owning part of the mine itself.

Sometimes the state takes the mine itself. Grasberg, in the highlands of Indonesian Papua, was run for half a century by the American company Freeport-McMoRan. Since December 2018, Indonesian state-owned and regional interests have held 51.24 percent of it, and Freeport the rest, though Freeport still runs it. Indonesia got control of one of the world's richest mines; Freeport got the right to keep operating it for decades more. And the rock itself pushes back. Much of Grasberg is now mined underground, by block caving: the miners undercut a huge column of ore and let it collapse under its own weight into tunnels below. On the eighth of September 2025, a rush of wet mud flooded the workings and killed 7 workers. Grasberg's copper output fell from about 1,800 million pounds in 2024 to 1,015 million in 2025, and a phased restart is planned from 2026. A mine is not only a bet on the price; it is a bet on the rock, and the people inside it bear that risk first.

And sometimes a state does more than collect rent: it moves the whole market. Congo produces about three-quarters of the world's cobalt, a metal used in batteries, mostly as a by-product of its copper mines. In February 2025, with prices low, it banned cobalt exports outright. In October it replaced the ban with quotas: 96,600 tonnes a year for 2026 and 2027, less than half of the 230,000 tonnes its mines produced in 2025. The price of cobalt on the London Metal Exchange rose from about 12 dollars a pound in 2024 to about 15. That is a cartel of one. Indonesia took the opposite route. Since 2020 it has banned the export of raw nickel ore, so anyone who wanted its nickel had to build smelters in Indonesia, and Chinese companies did. Its mines produced 2.6 million tonnes of nickel in 2025, two-thirds of the world's. The flood of Indonesian nickel pushed prices down, and Australia's nickel mines, among the oldest in the business, could not compete. Its output fell by more than half in a single year, to 45 thousand tonnes, as one company after another put its mines on care and maintenance.
Critical: A mineral becomes critical when three things are true: modern life needs it, there is no easy substitute, and its supply is concentrated in a few places that could be cut off. Here is the third condition, measured. For each metal, the share of the world's mining done by its largest producer. Congo mines about 73 percent of the world's cobalt. China mines about 69 percent of the rare earths, and Indonesia about two-thirds of the nickel. Iron ore, lithium and copper are spread more widely, at least at the mine. But remember the refining: China refines almost half the world's copper, and much larger shares of lithium, cobalt and rare earths. On the seventh of November 2025, copper itself was added to the United States' official list of critical minerals. The metal of wires is now treated as a matter of national security.

Being critical does not make a metal a good business. Lithium shows why. About 88 percent of lithium now goes into batteries, and when electric car sales took off, battery makers scrambled for it. The price of battery-grade lithium carbonate went from about 12 thousand dollars a tonne in 2021 to 64 thousand in 2022. Albemarle, the biggest American producer, nearly tripled its revenue, to 9.6 billion dollars in 2023. But unlike copper, lithium can be brought into production fast: from brines in Chile and Argentina, from hard-rock mines in Australia, China, Zimbabwe and Mali. Mines that had been planned in the boom all came at once. World lithium mining rose by 31 percent in a single year, the price collapsed to about 9 thousand dollars, and Albemarle lost money in 2024 and again in 2025. A critical mineral is critical to its buyers. To its producers it is still a commodity, with a cost curve and a cycle.

The sharpest case is the rare earths: seventeen elements with odd names that make the strongest permanent magnets, the ones inside wind turbines, electric motors, hard drives and guided missiles. They are not actually rare, but China mines about 69 percent of them and dominates their separation and refining. The United States mines some, at Mountain Pass in California, but 71 percent of its imports of rare-earth compounds and metals came from China. In April 2025, China put export controls on seven of them. In October it added five more. In November, it suspended the October controls for a year, while keeping April's. A single government, by licensing a few hundred thousand tonnes of oxide, could slow car factories on other continents. That is what makes a mineral critical: not its price, but who can turn off the tap.
Gold: Gold is the strangest metal in this film, because almost none of it is used up. The world's mines produced about 3,300 tonnes of gold in 2025. Gold is so dense that all of it would fit in a cube about 5.5 metres on a side, a little taller than three people standing on each other's shoulders. Yet at 2025's average price of 3,300 dollars an ounce, a record, that cube was worth about 350 billion dollars. Gold miners dig up far more value per tonne of metal than anyone in this film, and they do it from ore that often holds only a few grams of gold in a tonne of rock.

So where does it go? About forty percent into jewellery, and a quarter into bars that people and investors simply store. And about a fifth to central banks and other institutions. Central banks have been buying gold in large amounts; many analysts think one reason is to hold reserves that no other government can freeze. With that buying, the price climbed from about eighteen hundred dollars an ounce in 2021 and 2022 to 3,300 in 2025, thirty-eight percent up on the year before. Gold's price is not set by a cost curve or by factories' demand. It is set by fear, by interest rates, and by what people expect others to pay.

For the gold miners, the price rise has been a bonanza. Here is Newmont, the biggest of them, since 2012. Through the 2010s, as gold fell and then drifted, its revenue shrank and it lost money in several years. It bought its rivals Goldcorp in 2019 and Newcrest in 2023, and the costs of those deals and of lower-quality mines weighed on its profits. Then the price took off. Newmont's revenue went from 11.8 billion dollars in 2023 to 22.7 billion in 2025, and its net income to 7.1 billion, a record. The mines did not change much. The ounces did not change much. The price did. And remember Grasberg, whose gold made its copper cost less than nothing: in this market a copper mine with gold in its ore has a second business inside it.
Landscape: So here is the landscape, as of November 2026. Each bubble is a mining company that files its accounts with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, placed by its revenue in its latest financial year and by how much of that revenue it kept as profit. The two giants, Rio Tinto and BHP, each sold more than fifty billion dollars, mostly iron ore, and kept about a sixth of it. Vale, the third iron ore giant, kept much less. Freeport sells more copper than almost anyone, but much of Grasberg's and Cerro Verde's profit belongs to its partners, including the Indonesian state, and the mud rush hurt. Southern Copper, with mines in Peru and Mexico, kept almost a third of its revenue. Newmont, riding the gold price, did as well. And Albemarle, the lithium producer, is still losing money. Some of the biggest names are not here, because they do not file with the SEC: Chile's state-owned Codelco, Glencore, Anglo American, China's Zijin, and Barrick. Since those accounts closed, copper has risen to a record in dollars, about 14,473 a tonne in September 2026, while iron ore has stayed around a hundred.

And here is what to watch. Escondida's grade, falling towards point eight five percent this year. Grasberg's restart after the mud rush. Congo's cobalt quotas, which run through 2027. China's rare-earth controls, half of which are only suspended. And the gap between New York's copper price and London's, which measures how much the world expects American tariffs to matter. Every one of those is a story about rock, or about a state, and none of them is about the demand for copper, which keeps rising regardless.
Called: Part nine's forecast to test is the most famous bet in economics. In 1980 the biologist Paul Ehrlich, who had warned that a growing population would exhaust the Earth's resources, accepted a challenge from the economist Julian Simon, who believed that human ingenuity would always find more. On the twenty-ninth of September 1980 they agreed on a notional basket: two hundred dollars each of chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten, chosen by Ehrlich and his colleagues. If the basket was worth more after inflation in 1990, Simon would pay the difference; if less, Ehrlich would. All five fell. Tin and tungsten lost more than two-thirds of their real value. In October 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a cheque for 576 dollars 07. Using the Geological Survey's yearly average prices, we get the same verdict: the thousand-dollar basket fell to about 625 dollars.

Simon won. But was he right, or lucky? We can check, because the Geological Survey publishes a price for each of these metals for every year since 1900. So run the same bet, with the same five metals, for every ten-year window: 1900 to 1910, 1901 to 1911, and so on, 110 windows in all. Red means the basket rose in real terms and Ehrlich would have won; blue means it fell and Simon would have won. Here is 1980, the real bet: blue. But over the whole century, Ehrlich would have won 67 of the 110 windows, 61 percent. Simon picked a decade in which metal prices fell. Over the long run, the honest answer is the one from the intermission: prices swing in long cycles around a level that barely moves, because each boom brings new mines and new methods. Neither man's theory beats the cycle.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. Escondida produced 1,305 thousand tonnes in the year to June 2025. BHP's guidance for the year to June 2026 is 1,150 to 1,250. Its outlook for the five years after that is nine hundred thousand to a million tonnes a year. Our call: in the year to June 2027, Escondida will produce less than 1,100 thousand tonnes. We give it a 75 percent chance. The grade is falling, and BHP's own outlook sits below the line. What could make us wrong: the mine beat expectations in 2025 with more leaching and faster milling, and BHP has strong reasons to push throughput while copper is at a record. BHP will report the number in August 2027, and we will put it here, right or wrong.
